# ARIMA models

## ARIMA models

ARIMA models describe the autocorrelations in the data: how each observation relates to past observations and past errors.

An ARIMA model is rarely interpretable in terms of visible data structures like trend and seasonality. But it can capture a huge range of time series patterns.

## Stationarity

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
If $\{y_t\}$ is a stationary time series, then for all $s$, the distribution of $(y_t,\dots,y_{t+s})$ does not depend on $t$.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A **stationary series** is:

* roughly horizontal
* constant variance
* no patterns predictable in the long-term
:::

## Stationary? {.nostretch}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.2
gafa_stock |>
  filter(Symbol == "GOOG", year(Date) == 2018) |>
  autoplot(Close) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Closing price ($US)", title = "Google closing stock price")
```

::: {.poll #stationary-goog prompt="Is the Google closing stock price stationary?"}
- [ ] Yes
- [x] No
:::

## Stationary? {.nostretch}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.2
gafa_stock |>
  filter(Symbol == "GOOG", year(Date) == 2018) |>
  autoplot(difference(Close)) +
  labs(x = "Date", y = "Change ($US)", title = "Daily change in Google closing stock price")
```

::: {.poll #stationary-goog-diff prompt="Is the daily change in Google closing stock price stationary?"}
- [x] Yes
- [ ] No
:::

## Differencing

::: {.callout-note}
## Differences
First difference: $y'_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$

Second difference: $y''_t = y'_t - y'_{t-1} = y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}$

Seasonal difference: $y_t - y_{t-m}$, where $m$ is the seasonal period
:::

* Differencing helps to **stabilise the mean**.
* The differenced series is the change between each observation in the original series.
* Occasionally the differenced data will not appear stationary and it may be necessary to difference the data a second time.
* In practice, it is almost never necessary to go beyond second-order differences.

## Autoregressive models

::: {.callout-note}
## Autoregressive (AR) models
$$
  y_{t} = c + \phi_{1}y_{t - 1} + \phi_{2}y_{t - 2} + \cdots + \phi_{p}y_{t - p} + \varepsilon_{t},
$$
where $\varepsilon_t$ is white noise. A multiple regression with **lagged values** of $y_t$ as predictors.
:::

```{r}
#| label: arp
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.3
set.seed(1)
p1 <- tsibble(idx = seq_len(100), sim = 10 + arima.sim(list(ar = -0.8), n = 100), index = idx) |>
  autoplot(sim) + labs(x = "time", y = "", title = "AR(1): φ₁ = -0.8")
p2 <- tsibble(idx = seq_len(100), sim = 20 + arima.sim(list(ar = c(1.3, -0.7)), n = 100), index = idx) |>
  autoplot(sim) + labs(x = "time", y = "", title = "AR(2): φ₁ = 1.3, φ₂ = -0.7")
p1 + p2
```

* Cyclic behaviour is possible when $p\ge 2$.

## Moving average models

::: {.callout-note}
## Moving average (MA) models
$$
  y_{t} = c + \varepsilon_t + \theta_{1}\varepsilon_{t - 1} + \theta_{2}\varepsilon_{t - 2} + \cdots + \theta_{q}\varepsilon_{t - q},
$$
where $\varepsilon_t$ is white noise.
A multiple regression with **lagged errors** as predictors. Don't confuse with moving average smoothing!
:::

```{r}
#| label: maq
#| fig-height: 2.3
#| echo: false
set.seed(2)
p1 <- tsibble(idx = seq_len(100), sim = 20 + arima.sim(list(ma = 0.8), n = 100), index = idx) |>
  autoplot(sim) + labs(x = "time", y = "", title = "MA(1): θ₁ = 0.8")
p2 <- tsibble(idx = seq_len(100), sim = 20 + arima.sim(list(ma = c(-1, +0.8)), n = 100), index = idx) |>
  autoplot(sim) + labs(x = "time", y = "", title = "MA(2): θ₁ = -1, θ₂ = 0.8")

p1 + p2
```

## ARIMA models

::: {.callout-note}
## Autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models
$$\begin{aligned}
  y_{t} &= c + \phi_{1}y_{t - 1} + \cdots + \phi_{p}y_{t - p} \\
        & \qquad + \theta_{1}\varepsilon_{t - 1} + \cdots + \theta_{q}\varepsilon_{t - q} + \varepsilon_{t}.
\end{aligned}$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
* Predictors include both lagged values of $y_t$ and lagged errors.
:::

::: {.fragment}
### Autoregressive integrated moving average models

* Combine ARMA model with differencing.
* $d$-differenced series follows an ARMA model.
* Need to choose $p$, $d$, $q$ and whether or not to include $c$.
:::

## ARIMA models

::: {.callout-note}
## ARIMA($p, d, q$) model

| | |
|---:|:---|
| AR: | $p =$ order of the autoregressive part |
| I: | $d =$ degree of first differencing involved |
| MA: | $q =$ order of the moving average part. |
:::

* White noise model: ARIMA(0,0,0)
* Random walk: ARIMA(0,1,0) with no constant
* Random walk with drift: ARIMA(0,1,0) with const.
* AR($p$): ARIMA($p$,0,0)
* MA($q$): ARIMA(0,0,$q$)

## Example: National populations

```{r}
#| label: popfit2
#| echo: true
fit_pop <- global_economy |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(Population))
fit_pop
```

## Example: National populations

```{r}
#| label: popfit3
#| echo: true
fit_pop |>
  filter(Country == "Australia") |>
  report()
```

::: {.alertblock .fragment}
With $d=2$ the MA(1) model is for the second differences $y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}$, so
$$y_t = 2y_{t-1} - y_{t-2} - 0.661 \varepsilon_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \text{NID}(0, 4.06\times10^9)$$
:::

## Understanding ARIMA models

$c$ is the constant in the ARMA model for the $d$-times differenced series.

* If $c=0$ and $d=0$, the long-term forecasts will go to zero.
* If $c=0$ and $d=1$, the long-term forecasts will go to a non-zero constant.
* If $c=0$ and $d=2$, the long-term forecasts will follow a straight line.
* If $c\ne0$ and $d=0$, the long-term forecasts will go to the mean of the data.
* If $c\ne0$ and $d=1$, the long-term forecasts will follow a straight line.
* If $c\ne0$ and $d=2$, the long-term forecasts will follow a quadratic trend.

## Understanding ARIMA models

### Forecast variance and $d$
  * The higher the value of $d$, the more rapidly the prediction intervals increase in size.
  * For $d=0$, the long-term forecast standard deviation will go to the standard deviation of the historical data.

## Example: National populations

```{r}
#| label: popfc2
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 3.4
fit_pop |>
  forecast(h = 10) |>
  filter(Country == "Australia") |>
  autoplot(global_economy) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M"))
```

## How does ARIMA() work?

::: {.callout-important}
## Hyndman and Khandakar (JSS, 2008) algorithm

* Select the number of seasonal differences $D$ via a seasonal strength test, then the number of differences $d$ via KPSS tests.
* Select $p$, $q$ (and $P$, $Q$ for seasonal models) and inclusion of $c$ by minimising AICc.
* Use stepwise search to traverse model space.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.block}
$$\text{AICc} = -2 \log(L) + 2(p+q+k+1)\left[1 + \frac{(p+q+k+2)}{T-p-q-k-2}\right]$$
where $L$ is the maximised likelihood fitted to the *differenced* data,
$k=1$ if $c\neq 0$ and $k=0$ otherwise.
:::

Note: Can't compare AICc for different values of $d$.
:::

## How does ARIMA() work?

Step 1:
: Select current model (with smallest AICc) from:\
ARIMA$(2,d,2)$, ARIMA$(0,d,0)$, ARIMA$(1,d,0)$, ARIMA$(0,d,1)$

::: {.fragment}
Step 2:
: Consider variations of current model:

    * vary one of $p$, $q$ from current model by $\pm1$;
    * $p$, $q$ both vary from current model by $\pm1$;
    * include/exclude $c$ from current model.

Model with lowest AICc becomes current model.
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Repeat Step 2 until no lower AICc can be found.]{.alert}
:::

```{r}
#| label: ARMAgridsearch
#| include: false
start <- tribble(
  ~p, ~q,
  0, 0,
  1, 0,
  0, 1,
  2, 2
)
selected <- tribble(
  ~p, ~q,
  2, 2,
  3, 3,
  4, 2
)
griddf <- expand_grid(p = 0:6, q = 0:6) |>
  left_join(start |> mutate(start = TRUE), by = c("p", "q")) |>
  left_join(selected |> mutate(chosen = TRUE), by = c("p", "q")) |>
  replace_na(list(start = FALSE, chosen = FALSE)) |>
  mutate(
    step = case_when(
      start ~ 1,
      (p - selected$p[1])^2 + (q - selected$q[1])^2 <= 2 ~ 2,
      (p - selected$p[2])^2 + (q - selected$q[2])^2 <= 2 ~ 3,
      (p - selected$p[3])^2 + (q - selected$q[3])^2 <= 2 ~ 4
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(
    selected |>
      mutate(step = row_number() + 1) |>
      rename(fromp = p, fromq = q),
    by = "step"
  ) |>
  mutate(step = as.character(step))

# Models considered up to step k: arrows from the previous best model, with the
# best model so far circled
plot_grid_step <- function(k) {
  steps <- as.character(seq_len(k))
  griddf |>
    ggplot(aes(x = q, y = p)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2, colour = "gray", size = 5, shape = 19) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = fromq, y = fromp, xend = q, yend = p, col = step),
      data = griddf |> filter(step == as.character(k)),
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "inches"), type = "open"),
      linewidth = 1, lineend = "butt"
    ) +
    geom_point(aes(col = step),
      size = 5, shape = 19,
      data = griddf |> filter(step %in% steps)
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = griddf |> filter(step %in% steps, chosen),
      size = 12, shape = 21, stroke = 1.4
    ) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = 0:6) +
    scale_x_continuous(position = "top", breaks = 0:6) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
      axis.title.x = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0),
      axis.title.y = element_text(
        size = 12, hjust = 1,
        angle = 0, margin = margin(t = 0, r = 10, b = 0, l = 0)
      ),
      legend.position = "none"
    ) +
    scale_colour_manual(
      breaks = paste(1:4),
      values = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#CC79A7")
    )
}
```

# Seasonal ARIMA models

## Seasonal ARIMA models

$$\text{ARIMA}~\underbrace{(p,d,q)}_{\text{Non-seasonal part}}~\underbrace{(P,D,Q)_m}_{\text{Seasonal part}}$$

  * $m =$ seasonal period (e.g. 12 for monthly data, 4 for quarterly data).
  * $d$ first differences, $D$ seasonal differences
  * $p$ AR order, $q$ MA order
  * $P$ seasonal AR order, $Q$ seasonal MA order

::: {.alertblock}
Seasonal and non-seasonal terms combine multiplicatively
:::

## Corticosteroid drug sales

Monthly Australian Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) expenditure on corticosteroid (H02) drugs.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 3
h02 <- PBS |>
  filter(ATC2 == "H02") |>
  summarise(Cost = sum(Cost) / 1e6)
h02 |> autoplot(Cost) + labs(y = "$AUD million")
```

## Corticosteroid drug sales: log transform

```{r}
#| echo: true
h02 |> autoplot(log(Cost))
```

## Corticosteroid drug sales: seasonal difference

```{r}
#| echo: true
h02 |> autoplot(log(Cost) |> difference(12))
```

## Corticosteroid drug sales: seasonal and first difference

```{r}
#| echo: true
h02 |> autoplot(log(Cost) |> difference(12) |> difference(1))
```

## Corticosteroid drug sales: automatic ARIMA

```{r}
#| label: h02fit
#| echo: true
fit_h02 <- h02 |>
  model(auto = ARIMA(log(Cost)))
fit_h02 |> report()
```

::: {.fragment}
$d=1$ and $D=1$ match the differencing above, leaving an AR(2) and a seasonal MA(1) at lag 12.
:::

## Corticosteroid drug sales: manual ARIMA

Specify the orders with `pdq()` and `PDQ()`, and the constant with `0 +` (exclude) or `1 +` (include).

```{r}
#| label: h02manual
#| echo: true
h02 |>
  model(manual = ARIMA(log(Cost) ~ 0 + pdq(2, 1, 0) + PDQ(0, 1, 1))) |>
  report()
```

::: {.fragment}
Orders can be chosen manually by inspecting the ACF and PACF of the differenced data.
:::

## Corticosteroid drug sales: forecasts

```{r}
#| label: h02fcst
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 2.8
fit_h02 |>
  forecast(h = "3 years") |>
  autoplot(h02) +
  labs(y = "$AUD million")
```

## Corticosteroid drug sales: searching harder

By default `ARIMA()` takes shortcuts to keep model selection fast.

::: {.callout-note}
## Search options

* `stepwise = FALSE`: fit every model within the order limit, not just the stepwise path.
* `approximation = FALSE`: estimate with the exact likelihood rather than an approximation.
* `order_constraint`: limit the total number of AR and MA terms considered.
:::

A wider search is slower, but may find a model with a lower AICc.

## Corticosteroid drug sales: searching harder {.code-small}

```{r}
#| label: h02tryharder
#| echo: true
fit_h02_best <- h02 |>
  model(best = ARIMA(log(Cost),
    stepwise = FALSE,
    approximation = FALSE,
    order_constraint = p + q + P + Q <= 9
  ))
fit_h02_best |> report()
```

::: {.fragment}
Same differencing and transformation, so the AICc is comparable: $-487$ vs $-483$ for the automatic model, using nine coefficients instead of three.
:::

## Corticosteroid drug sales: residuals

```{r}
#| label: h02resid
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 3.2
gg_tsresiduals(fit_h02_best, lag_max = 36)
```

## Corticosteroid drug sales: residuals

Ljung-Box tests, with `dof` set to the number of estimated coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: h02lb
#| echo: true
bind_rows(
  augment(fit_h02) |> features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 36, dof = 3),
  augment(fit_h02_best) |> features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 36, dof = 9)
)
```

::: {.fragment}
The automatic model leaves autocorrelation in its residuals; the wider search does not, so we prefer it.
:::

## Corticosteroid drug sales: forecasts

```{r}
#| label: h02f
#| echo: true
#| fig-height: 2.8
fit_h02_best |>
  forecast(h = "3 years") |>
  autoplot(h02) +
  labs(y = "$AUD million")
```


# Forecast ensembles

## Forecast ensembles {.code-small}

```{r}
#| label: trainall
#| echo: true
train <- tourism |>
  filter(year(Quarter) <= 2014)
fit_tourism <- train |>
  model(
    ets = ETS(Trips),
    arima = ARIMA(Trips),
    snaive = SNAIVE(Trips)
  ) |>
  mutate(mixed = (ets + arima + snaive) / 3)
```

* Fits three models to each of the 304 tourism series (this takes a while).
* Ensemble forecast `mixed` is a simple average of the three fitted models.
* `forecast()` will produce distributional forecasts taking into account the correlations between the forecast errors of the component models.

## Forecast ensembles

```{r}
#| label: trainfc
#| dependson: "trainall"
#| fig-height: 3.6
fc <- fit_tourism |> forecast(h = "3 years")
fc |>
  filter(Region == "Snowy Mountains", Purpose == "Holiday") |>
  autoplot(tourism |> filter(year(Quarter) >= 2010), level = NULL)
```

## Forecast ensembles

Accuracy on the 2015--2017 test set, averaged across all series.

```{r}
#| label: trainacc
#| dependson: "trainfc"
fc |>
  accuracy(tourism) |>
  group_by(.model) |>
  summarise(RMSE = mean(RMSE), MASE = mean(MASE)) |>
  arrange(RMSE)
```

::: {.fragment}
Averaging lets errors from different models partially cancel, and reduces the risk of picking the wrong model.
:::
